title: Ledger and Harbor
premise: In 1913, Jonah Blackwood drives for suffragist organizer Edith Marlowe and secretly reads every letter she carries, convinced history belongs to other people. When the army requisitions their coastal town to suppress a dockworkers' strike, Edith's ledger — the only record of every name the soldiers have disappeared — becomes both evidence and death sentence. Jonah must smuggle it past three military checkpoints to a journalist in the city, discovering along the way that memory kept by ordinary hands is itself an act of rebellion. She reaches the press at terrible cost: Edith is arrested in her place, and Jonah, once a bystander, chooses to stay and testify under her own name.
about_author: Cyrus Dunmore is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing forgotten letters in provincial record offices. Ledger and Harbor is a novel born from the marginalia of people history never bothered to name.

chapters.title: The Weight of Other People's Words
chapters.summary: Jonah Blackwood, driver and self-appointed reader of Edith Marlowe's correspondence, delivers letters through the fog-bound harbor town while insisting to herself that suffrage, strikes, and scandal are affairs for bolder souls. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: wry detachment masking loneliness; she belongs everywhere as staff and nowhere as herself.

chapters.title: A Ledger of Small Names
chapters.summary: Edith reveals the ledger she keeps: every dockworker threatened, every woman blacklisted, every name the shipping company wants erased. She calls it insurance. Jonah calls it suicide written in ink. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: first crack in her detachment — she recognizes her own father's name among the entries.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: At dawn, soldiers occupy the town hall, the pier, and the telegraph office. A colonel announces martial law 'for the duration of the labor dispute.' Edith's house is searched; the ledger is not found because Jonah, on instinct, has hidden it in the spare tire well of the motorcar. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: fear arriving late, then all at once.

chapters.title: The Colonel's Courtesy
chapters.summary: Colonel Ashworth pays a courteous, menacing visit, offering Edith protection in exchange for 'any documents bearing names.' Jonah serves tea with steady hands while understanding they are being measured for coffins. POV: alternating Jonah and Edith. Emotional beat: the horror of politeness as a weapon.

chapters.title: Checkpoint One: The Bridge
chapters.summary: Jonah volunteers to carry the ledger to journalist Samuel Reeve in the city, ninety miles away. At the bridge checkpoint a young sergeant searches the car but waves her through after she flirts and lies about delivering laundry. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: exhilaration curdling into shame — she got lucky, not good.

chapters.title: Letters I Should Not Have Read
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter: three years of stolen reading — love letters, begging letters, a widow's confession — and how each one quietly taught Jonah that private lives are where history actually lives. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: tender, elegiac; the origin of her compulsion and her conscience.

chapters.title: The Man Who Waits at Harrow Lane
chapters.summary: Jonah meets Tom Quill, a strike organizer she has driven past a hundred times without speaking. He knows what the ledger means and offers to move with her as cover — a couple traveling to a wedding. Old attraction, long suppressed by duty, resurfaces. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: warmth and guilt entangled.

chapters.title: What the Soldiers Took
chapters.summary: News from home: Edith has been detained 'for questioning.' The town's women organize silent vigils; the colonel bans gatherings of more than three. Jonah realizes the ledger is now the only voice Edith has left. POV: alternating Jonah and vigil organizer Mrs. Penhale. Emotional beat: grief hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Two: The Garrison Road
chapters.summary: Traveling with Tom, Jonah faces a full vehicle search at the garrison road. The ledger, sewn into the lining of her coat, survives; Tom's forged papers do not. He is taken aside. She must drive on alone or be caught with him. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: the sick arithmetic of survival — leaving him behind to save the names.

chapters.title: A Night Without a Harbor
chapters.summary: Alone in a roadside inn, Jonah reads the ledger properly for the first time, entry by entry, and weeps over strangers. A maid warns her the innkeeper reports to the army. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: transformation — the names stop being evidence and become people she is responsible to.

chapters.title: The Informer's Face
chapters.summary: Jonah discovers the leak: Edith's own clerk, bribed with his brother's debts, told the colonel about the ledger's existence. She confronts him; he begs; she neither forgives nor condemns him, but memorizes his face. POV: Jonah with a brief clerk interlude. Emotional beat: moral complexity — even betrayal has a hostage's logic.

chapters.title: Edith, Interrogated
chapters.summary: In a cell, Edith endures questioning designed to break her sense of her own significance. She recites the ledger entries from memory, turning interrogation into testimony. POV: Edith. Emotional beat: defiant dignity; the theme of memory as resistance made flesh.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three: The Ferry Gate
chapters.summary: The final barrier before the city: a ferry checkpoint where officers cross-reference passenger lists against wanted notices. Jonah gives the ledger to an unexpected ally — the young sergeant from the bridge, whose sister's name is in its pages. POV: Jonah and the sergeant. Emotional beat: trust as a leap made in the dark.

chapters.title: Samuel Reeve's Narrow Office
chapters.summary: Jonah reaches Reeve, who reads the ledger in silence and then tells her the truth: publication will trigger reprisals against everyone named, including Edith. Evidence alone saves no one; witnesses are needed. POV: Jonah and Reeve. Emotional beat: the floor dropping out — smuggling was the easy part.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Tom escapes custody and finds her; they spend one stolen night planning whether to flee together to Canada or stay. Duty pulls them opposite ways — he to the striking docks, she to the witness stand. POV: alternating Jonah and Tom. Emotional beat: aching tenderness; choosing each other without choosing escape.

chapters.title: The Town Remembers
chapters.summary: Reeve's article runs. The named families of the harbor town, emboldened, begin giving sworn statements; Mrs. Penhale organizes testimony the army cannot arrest fast enough. POV: Mrs. Penhale and townsfolk ensemble. Emotional beat: rising collective courage — history happening to these people, by these people.

chapters.title: Ashworth's Reckoning
chapters.summary: Colonel Ashworth, facing inquiry, moves to destroy the remaining records and deport Edith before she can testify. Jonah learns the transport schedule from the informer's guilty confession. POV: Jonah and Ashworth. Emotional beat: cold dread; the antagonist's desperate, plausible logic.

chapters.title: The Rescue That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Jonah and Tom attempt to intercept Edith's transport; the plan half-fails — they free her, but Tom is shot covering the retreat and dies in Jonah's arms at the harbor edge. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: devastating climax; love's cost paid in full.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: At the inquiry, Jonah speaks under her own name for the first time — not as a driver, not as a reader of others' letters, but as a witness. Edith corroborates from memory. Ashworth is relieved of command. POV: Jonah and Edith. Emotional beat: quiet triumph; a voice found and used.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Could Not Hold
chapters.summary: Jonah returns to the emptied harbor town, walks the checkpoints now unmanned, and adds Tom's name to the ledger's final page in her own handwriting. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: mourning braided with purpose; grief given a place to live.

chapters.title: Harbor Light
chapters.summary: Months later, the strike settled and the town half-healed, Edith reopens her organizing rooms with Jonah as partner, not employee. The ledger goes to the national archive under both their names. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: belonging achieved — she is no longer outside history, but one of its keepers.

chapters.title: Every Letter, Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Years afterward, an older Jonah addresses a hall of young organizers, reading aloud the names from the ledger so they are spoken rather than merely stored. She ends with Tom's. POV: Jonah, framed memoir. Emotional beat: resolution and transmission — memory passed hand to hand, the truest harbor.
